title: AI in Education #8: Five Things I Learned from Becky Allen
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton distills five takeaways from a conversation with education researcher Becky Allen, co-founder of Teacher Tapp and an evaluator at Alpha School. Allen offers calibrated optimism: AI will let us replicate proven best practice at scale, but it will not discover new ways to teach, because education has a “verification problem”—unlike chess or driving, you cannot instantly check whether deep, durable learning occurred, so reinforcement learning cannot crack teaching. The best current uses mirror what a great one-to-one tutor does: adaptive prerequisite-knowledge activation and guided, step-by-step worked examples. Khanmigo failed, she argues, because students take the path of least resistance, so effective platforms must tightly control the learning pathway. Alpha functions as a deliberately “benign laboratory,” and her prediction is understated: mainstream schools stay largely the same, marking gets solved, and software-powered micro-schools appear at the margins to serve students the current system fails.
points: AI will replicate best practice at scale but will not discover new pedagogy, because education’s “verification problem” prevents the reinforcement-learning loops that power AI breakthroughs elsewhere.
The most impressive current uses replicate a great one-to-one tutor: adaptive prerequisite-knowledge activation in free text, and guided worked examples revealed one step at a time.
Khanmigo failed because students take the path of least resistance; effective platforms must be highly controlled, deciding what students work on, in what order, and for how long.
Alpha School is valuable as a “benign laboratory”—you answer “can this work at all?” in low-risk circumstances before asking “can this work for everyone?”
Allen predicts mainstream schools change little, but marking gets largely solved and software-powered micro-schools emerge at the margins for persistently absent and home-educated students.
quotes: AI will allow us to take what we already understand about effective teaching and build it into apps that can deliver that practice to every student, consistently, at scale
But in education, we cannot cut open a student’s brain and check what happened.
when you ask children what they want to do, they do not choose the most efficient and productive activities for learning
you should build in benign circumstances to figure out what works without worrying that you are damaging vulnerable children
Not a revolution. More like a slow, quiet expansion of what is possible for the students the current system cannot serve.
